edits.old: Watch memory and cache pressure alongside storage growth. Percona's dashboard compares WiredTiger cache use with its maximum and says sustained near-full use increases eviction; sustained page faults can mean the working dataset exceeds host memory and must be read from disk. MongoDB's manual also treats rising page faults or growing data changed but not yet written as signs of memory pressure. (high confidence)
edits.new: Watch memory and cache pressure alongside storage growth. Percona's dashboard compares WiredTiger cache use with its maximum and says a Used line that hugs the Max line means eviction pressure is constant; a sustained high page-fault rate can mean the working dataset has outgrown host memory and must be read from disk. Percona also says a large fraction of dirty pages means changes are generated faster than MongoDB can write them to disk. MongoDB's serverStatus documentation says the page fault counter may increase dramatically during poor performance and may correlate with limited memory and larger data sets. Sources: https://docs.percona.com/percona-monitoring-and-management/3/reference/dashboards/dashboard-mongodb-wiredtiger-details.html ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/serverStatus.md

evidence.quote: A Used line that hugs the Max line means the cache is always full and eviction pressure is constant.
A sustained high rate tells you that your working dataset has outgrown the available memory on this host.
If dirty pages make up a large fraction of the total, your workload is generating changes faster than MongoDB can write them to disk.
may increase dramatically during moments of poor performance and may correlate with limited memory environments and larger data sets.

edits.old: For Atlas Search, monitor search-index size separately from source collection size because mappings and features can change their size ratio. MongoDB recommends establishing a normal index-size and growth-rate baseline, watching unexplained jumps or sustained growth above that rate and declining free disk, and reserving room for the largest index plus expected growth and rebuilds. (high confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-12)
edits.new: For Atlas Search, monitor search-index size as its own metric, because index configuration options can make an index many times larger than the size of the data. MongoDB's Atlas Search monitoring guidance recommends establishing a baseline for typical index size, growth rate and reserved free disk; watching for sudden jumps that don't match data or schema changes, sustained climbs above the usual growth rate, and free disk trending toward the alert threshold; and sizing Search nodes to hold the largest index plus expected growth, with headroom for index builds and rebuilds. Sources: https://medium.com/mongodb/monitoring-atlas-search-the-key-metrics-66c90c39d480 ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/performance/index-performance.md

evidence.quote: Start by establishing a baseline for what “normal” looks like in your environment — typical index size, typical growth rate, and the amount of free disk you expect to keep in reserve.
Sudden jumps in index size that don’t line up with an obvious change in your data volume or schema.
A good rule of thumb is to size your Search nodes so they comfortably hold your largest index plus the growth runway you expect between scaling reviews.
Some index configuration options can lead to indexes that take up a significant proportion of your disk space. In some cases, your index could be many times larger than the size of your data.
